body_markdown:
You know what “silly season” is, right?


For those who don’t, it’s a usually harmless, seemingly annual phenomenon that occurs in sports—NASCAR, for example—around the time the current season begins to wind down and talk turns to next year. Often, peculiar things happen that may seem silly on the surface, but are destined to affect next year’s competition. Like the out-of-nowhere announcement that former Cup champion Brad Keselowski won’t be driving for RFK Racing, a team in which he is the “K” in RFK.


Yeah, that qualifies as a silly season surprise. But not by a long shot does it top the Official Silly Season Points Leader: Broken last Tuesday[by The Athletic](https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/7685423/2026/10/13/dodge-nascar-cup-series-return-2027/) , it’s the rumor that Dodge, after a 15-year absence, will return to NASCAR Cup racing.


Getty Images


Wait, that isn’t news, or even surprising: Tim Kuniskis has been saying that for weeks. Kuniskis is Head of American Brands and North America Marketing, plus being the Head of SRT Performance, according to his official Stellantis biography. Keep reading that biography and you’ll see no mention that Kuniskis, after 32 years with the company, “retired” in May of 2024.


Why am I using quotation marks around “retired?” Because there’s a huge difference between saying an executive “retired,” or “was retired.” Stellantis doubled down on making it sound as though it was *all Tim’s idea! We begged him to stay!* But a trophy-sized salmon, or trout, or bass, or presumably some other big fish, came a-calling!


Inside the company, nobody I knew bought that. The problem, they said, was that Stellantis CEO Carlos Tavares told Kuniskis that the fun’s over, nobody wants Hellcats, they want electric vehicles, and they want them *now!* That opinion may have been bolstered by like-minded members of the media, who possibly lived in New York City, San Francisco, Los Angeles, Austin, and even Detroit: I live in a city called General Population, and my opinion differed, based on real life. I walk out on my porch and look left, and that’s Jim; he bought a C8 Corvette. I look right, and that neighbor, also named Jim, bought a diesel pickup.


[Cameron Neveu](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/cameron-neveu/)


No one is saying that investing in an electric future isn’t smart. But any farmer knows you have to feed the cow you’re milking. Dodge produced a very handsome, eighth-generation Charger that drove really well. It was electric. Nobody bought them.


Six months after Kuniskis walked, a press release that Stellantis hoped you wouldn’t read too closely said that he was returning to Stellantis as CEO of the Ram truck brand. That was one week after his boss at Stellantis, Carlos Tavares, “retired.”


Seven months after Kuniskis was un-retired, he was the head of not only Ram, but everything Stellantis sells in America, including Chrysler, Jeep, Alfa-Romeo, Fiat, Maserati and, of course, Dodge. Kuniskis is also the head of marketing, too.


Stellantis


Bottom line: If Tim Kuniskis wants back in NASCAR, Dodge is headed to NASCAR.


But this is where we circle back to NASCAR Silly Season. As I said, the proclamation that Dodge wants back in NASCAR’s top series isn’t news. But this is: They apparently want to start with the season-opening Daytona 500 on February 21, barely four months away.


That’s silly, alright. But this is sillier, times 10: The engine Dodge will race is a Chevrolet that essentially, I’m guessing, might have an air cleaner and a pair of valve covers that say “Dodge,” but it will be built by ECR Engines, which stands for Earnhardt Childress Racing, which already builds Chevrolet engines used in Cup racing, and apparently will continue to build Chevrolet Cup engines.


ECR is owned by 81-year-old Richard Childress. This is what it says on the Richard Childress Racing website: “Our headquarters is also home to ECR Engines, a subsidiary of RCR that provides high-performance motors to us, and other Chevrolet teams in NASCAR’s top three national series… ECR has also reached success in the IMSA WeatherTech SportsCar Championship Series powering the Cadillac DPi-V.R.” That’s a strong General Motors connection.


Richard Childress looks on during qualifying for the NASCAR Cup Series Daytona 500 at Daytona International Speedway on February 11, 2026.


Patrick McDermott/Getty Images


And NASCAR in general, and Chevrolet in particular, are fine with this? When Kaulig Racing signed up to develop, build, and field Ram trucks in the NASCAR series, they did, and still do, own a two-car Chevrolet team in the NASCAR Cup series. When notified of the Ram connection, Chevrolet pulled all support for Kaulig’s Cup cars, driven by A.J. Allmendinger (22nd in points after 32 races) and Todd Gilliland (23rd). Team members have said publicly that losing Chevy’s support has been detrimental.


Dodge won’t be much help at first, since it hasn’t had a serious racing program for years. They won the NASCAR Cup championship in 2012, with driver Brad Keselowski, and immediately quit NASCAR Cup racing. The next year, they won an IMSA sports car class championship with the Dodge Viper GTS-R, and quit that program. Stellantis chief designer Ralph Gilles, a man who loves racing and is an excellent amateur driver, ran that Viper program: He called ending it a “business decision.”


Brad Keselowski, driver of the #2 Miller Lite Dodge, and Marcos Ambrose, driver of the #9 Stanley Ford, battle for position during the NASCAR Sprint Cup Series Finger Lakes 355 at the Glen at Watkins Glen International on August 12, 2012.


John Harrelson/Getty Images


The rumor about the “Dodge” engine notes that ECR must somehow alter them, making the engines acceptably different from the Chevrolet. Like what? Valves? Pistons? Crankshaft? Block? Or just the writing on the valve covers and the color of the air cleaner?


Puzzling. NASCAR is scrupulous in how it makes sure the Ford, Chevrolet, and Toyota engine builders jump through hoops to create plausible deniability that all the NASCAR Cup V-8s are already pretty much the same. NASCAR is going to let Dodge into the executive playground without having to develop its own V-8?


Well, apparently they will. Several sources, who I consider to be pretty much unimpeachable, are saying, as one put it, “a 90% probability” of this happening just the way it’s being laid out.


Jamie Squire/Getty Images


So color me stunned, but the more I think about it, the more I wonder why I’m stunned. After all, while NASCAR doesn’t exactly advertise it, the engines in its ARCA and Craftsman Truck Series are identical spec engines: 6.4-liter V-8s built by Ilmor Engineering have been used in ARCA since 2015, and 6.2-liter Ilmor V-8s have been run in the NASCAR truck series since 2018. It’s accurate to say those fuel-injected Ilmor engines are inspired by the Chevrolet LS V-8, but they are different enough to free NASCAR from having to spend much time making sure they are legal, since the Ilmors are sealed, and teams aren’t allowed to work on them.


There’s still a rule that you can run those old, leftover, carbureted V-8s from the olden days, but few do: I asked if any of the starters in this year’s ARCA race at Daytona were using a grandfathered-in carbureted engine and was told all 40 cars had the Ilmor.


After the truck series went to the Ilmor engines, I spoke to several representatives of NASCAR O’Reilly and Cup series teams to see if they saw a day when NASCAR would allow identical, spec engines in those top two series. All said no; they couldn’t. “If they did,” said one Cup team owner, “what would the car manufacturers get out of going racing with an engine they didn’t develop?”


Jeff Bloxham/LAT Images


Of course, it has happened. Remember the odd-looking Nissan Deltawing race car? It actually made it to the 24 Hours of Le Mans in 2012, and though it only completed 75 laps before it crashed out, the Deltawing got far more publicity than the Audi R18 hybrid that won. This thrilled Nissan. Less thrilling may have been the fact that the Deltawing’s little four-cylinder engine, built by British Touring Car specialist Ray Mallock, contained more Chevrolet parts than Nissan parts, though I am positive it had a Nissan throttle body because I saw them bolt it on. Maybe we need a Stolen Valor Act for racecar engines.


Back to Dodge and the unretired Tim Kuniskis. I’m guessing that there are two possible reasons why Dodge will be allowed to enter a Charger that is running a redecorated Chevy V-8. One is because Dodge must have pledged to build its own NASCAR Cup V-8 by 2028 (almost impossible, I’m told), or 2029. Or even 2030, when NASCAR says it’ll have a new set of regulations.


Or two: That NASCAR has modified its standards in order to land its long-desired fourth manufacturer. Dodge will certainly pay an initiation fee that could total north of seven figures, and then expect Kuniskis—who, as mentioned, rules over the North American marketing budget—to absolutely melt Dodge’s portion of that in NASCAR Cup advertising and sponsorship, tied to the mildly refreshed, eighth-generation Charger Hellcat[that is so-strongly-rumored](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/report-v-8-hellcat-charger-will-return-in-2028/) for the 2028 model year.


It has long been a fact that it’s the engine requirement (as well as NASCAR’s long, *long* season) that has scared away manufacturers from joining NASCAR. Honda doesn’t even have a V-8. Genesis is going IMSA racing in the NASCAR-owned WeatherTech SportsCar Championship next year, and perhaps they can be lured to NASCAR without having to build an engine. (Worth noting: One of IMSA’s four WeatherTech classes uses a spec engine: all LMP2 cars have a British-built Gibson V-8). Volkswagen, with Michael Andretti, came very close to participating in NASCAR, but was stopped in its tracks[by Dieselgate.](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/ten-years-after-dieselgate-tdi-powered-vws-carry-a-premium/)


Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images


All that said, this is going to be challenging. Ram has at least logged almost a full season in NASCAR, but despite the common engine used by all teams, the five Ram trucks have scored only one top-five finish. They’ve gotten a lot of exposure in the Craftsman Truck Series (next year it’s the FedEx Freight Truck Series, but I’m not an early adopter), mostly from its innovative Ram guest driver program, which began in February at Daytona with three-time Cup champion Tony Stewart, who took a break from racing his Elite Motorsports NHRA Top Fuel dragster to compete in the brand-new Ram.


With Stewart and YouTube content over-provider Cleetus McFarland making his truck series debut at Daytona, the truck race had boffo ratings, despite McFarland crashing out on lap 5; he finished 37th in a 37-truck field. Stewart was knocked into the wall on lap 39, thus finishing 36th.


Other guest NASCAR Ram drivers have included IndyCar’s Conor Daly, former NASCAR racer and current broadcaster Regan Smith, and retired NASCAR racers Elliot Sadler and Ryan Newman.


James Gilbert/Getty Images


Stewart returns next week, driving the rotating “Free Agent” No. 25 Ram at Talladega Speedway on October 23. Given the buzz surrounding the presumably pending Dodge NASCAR Cup announcement, Kuniskis and his team would do well to get out in front of this quickly, and the Talladega weekend would be a ripe opportunity to announce any Daytona-and-beyond plans.


Might Kuniskis have Kaulig Racing prepare a third Cup car for a guest driver in the Daytona 500? Seems possible, but he or she likely would not have a chartered guaranteed starting spot, since Kaulig only owns two. And it wouldn’t be Stewart; he and his Tony Stewart Racing team, which is backed by Dodge, will be busy with the NHRA season opener at Pomona, which for some really silly reason is scheduled opposite the Daytona 500 on February 21.


But, if all this happens, expect more out-of-the-box marketing that Dodge seems to do so well.


Maybe it isn’t silly. But I need some convincing.
